# Dvedhāvitakka Sutta (MN 19 (PTS MN i 114))
**ID:** MN 19 (PTS MN i 114)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Dvedhāvitakka Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 114
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn19
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dvedhāvitakka Sutta* (MN 19, PTS MN i 114) recounts the Buddha's pre-awakening meditative training, in which he divided his thoughts (*vitakka*) into two categories: unwholesome thoughts of sensuality, ill will, and cruelty/harming, and wholesome thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*), non-ill will, and non-harming [Stanley et al. 2018; Hung 2010; Gaffney 2003]. He realized that whatever one frequently thinks shapes the inclination of the mind, and that unwholesome thoughts are harmful to oneself and others, destroy wisdom, and obstruct Nibbāna [Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2017]. The sutta illustrates this vigilant restraint through the simile of a cowherd minding his cattle when crops are ripe [Emmanuel 2017; Stanley et al. 2018]. He also found that even excessive reflection on wholesome thoughts made the body weary, prompting him to settle and unify the mind beyond discursive thought into *jhāna*, ultimately attaining the four absorptions and the three higher knowledges (*vijjā*) on the night of awakening [Hung 2010; Polak 2011; Gaffney 2003].
Unlike longer autobiographical accounts such as the *Mahāsaccaka Sutta* (MN 36), the *Dvedhāvitakka Sutta* and the *Bhayabherava Sutta* (MN 4) omit the Bodhisatta's study under early teachers and ascetic strivings, focusing directly on the immediate path to awakening [Gaffney 2003; Polak 2011; Wynne 2007]. Its full parallel is extant in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* as MĀ 102 (*Nian jing* 念經) [SuttaCentral; Hung 2010]. While the two versions share the same doctrinal framework and similes, the Chinese parallel places the cowherd simile prior to the exposition on mental inclination [Anālayo 2014]. The sutta is also referenced in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 1.1) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus indicates widespread textual reuse across the Pāli canon, sharing extensive formulaic passages on the *jhānas* and knowledges with MN 36, MN 4, MN 85, MN 100, the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 3 and AN 8), and the *Vinaya Piṭaka* [DharmaNexus; Shulman 2014]. DharmaNexus also aligns parts of the text with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, the Sarvāstivāda *Dharmaskandha*, and several Chinese and Tibetan texts [DharmaNexus; Almogi 2014].
